TRADE SECRET PRE-DISCOVERY IDENTIFICATION — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme Inc.

PURPOSE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This Information Sheet describes California Code of Civil Procedure section 2019.210, a civil-procedure statute that applies once a lawsuit alleging trade secret misappropriation under California's Uniform Trade Secrets Act (Civil Code section 3426 et seq.) has already been filed. It is prepared by Jane Doe concerning a case involving Acme Inc. and John Smith, identified by court case number 24CV012345 in Superior Court of California, County of Santa Clara, and concerning the following trade secret: the proprietary formulation described in the complaint. Section 2019.210 requires the party alleging misappropriation to identify the claimed trade secret with reasonable particularity before that party may begin discovery relating to the trade secret. This document explains what that statute's text says and does not say. It does not identify any trade secret with the particularity the statute requires, does not draft or file a trade secret identification statement, and does not evaluate whether any specific description of a trade secret meets the reasonable-particularity standard in a given case. This document is separate from, and does not repeat, the corpus's existing Trade Secret Misappropriation Cease and Desist Letter (which addresses the substantive definitions of misappropriation and improper means and the remedies for a completed violation), Trade Secret Preemption Doctrine Information Sheet (which addresses which other civil claims survive alongside a misappropriation claim), Criminal Trade Secret Theft Information Sheet and Economic Espionage Act Information Sheet (which address criminal liability), and the corpus's DTSA-focused NDA and cease-and-desist documents (which address the federal Defend Trade Secrets Act rather than this state civil-discovery statute). None of those documents describe the pre-discovery identification requirement covered here.

SCOPE: ACTIONS ALLEGING MISAPPROPRIATION UNDER THE UNIFORM TRADE SECRETS ACT
By its own text, Code of Civil Procedure section 2019.210 applies specifically "in any action alleging the misappropriation of a trade secret under the Uniform Trade Secrets Act," which the statute cross-references as Title 5, commencing with Civil Code section 3426. The section appears within the Civil Discovery Act, in the chapter governing the methods and sequence of discovery, as a discovery-sequencing rule tied to that specific type of state-law civil action.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "In any action alleging the misappropriation of a trade secret under the Uniform Trade Secrets Act (Title 5 (commencing with Section 3426) of Part 1 of Division 4 of the Civil Code)"
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 2019.210 (Leginfo official text), Cal. Civ. Proc. Code § 2019.210 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=2019.210.)
  Known gap: The statute's text does not state whether it applies of its own force to an action alleging misappropriation only under the federal Defend Trade Secrets Act and brought only in federal court, as opposed to a California Uniform Trade Secrets Act claim; that question depends on how a federal court treats a state procedural statute, which is outside this section's text and was not researched or verified in this session. This clause also does not address whether or how California trial courts apply an identification requirement in a case combining a California Uniform Trade Secrets Act claim with other claims.

REQUIREMENT TO IDENTIFY THE TRADE SECRET BEFORE DISCOVERY
Section 2019.210 states a sequencing rule: before the party alleging misappropriation may commence discovery relating to the claimed trade secret, that party must identify the trade secret with reasonable particularity. The identification requirement is expressly made "subject to any orders that may be appropriate under Section 3426.5 of the Civil Code," the companion provision addressing court-ordered secrecy protections.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "before commencing discovery relating to the trade secret, the party alleging the misappropriation shall identify the trade secret with reasonable particularity subject to any orders that may be appropriate under Section 3426.5 of the Civil Code."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 2019.210 (Leginfo official text), Cal. Civ. Proc. Code § 2019.210 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=2019.210.)
  Known gap: The statute's text does not specify the form the identification must take (for example, a standalone written statement versus a discovery response), does not set a numerical deadline, and does not itself define which discovery methods count as "discovery relating to the trade secret." Those procedural details are not addressed in the statutory text quoted here.

THE STATUTE'S TEXT DOES NOT DEFINE "REASONABLE PARTICULARITY"
The phrase "reasonable particularity" is the operative standard in section 2019.210, but the statute's text supplies no definition, list of required elements, or example of what identifying a trade secret with reasonable particularity looks like in practice.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "identify the trade secret with reasonable particularity"
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 2019.210 (Leginfo official text), Cal. Civ. Proc. Code § 2019.210 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=2019.210.)
  Known gap: How much detail satisfies "reasonable particularity" has reportedly been addressed in published California appellate decisions interpreting this section, but a case-law search on that question could not be completed in this research session: a CourtListener search for California case law discussing section 2019.210 and "reasonable particularity" returned a rate-limit error (HTTP 429, 125-request daily quota exhausted) before any result was retrieved. This document accordingly describes only the statute's own text and does not describe how courts have applied or elaborated the standard.

THE STATUTE'S TEXT DOES NOT STATE A CONSEQUENCE FOR NONCOMPLIANCE
Section 2019.210's operative sentence imposes the identification requirement but does not itself state what happens if the party alleging misappropriation proceeds with discovery relating to the trade secret without first identifying it with reasonable particularity. No sanction, dismissal, evidence-exclusion rule, or automatic stay is written into the text of this section.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "In any action alleging the misappropriation of a trade secret under the Uniform Trade Secrets Act (Title 5 (commencing with Section 3426) of Part 1 of Division 4 of the Civil Code), before commencing discovery relating to the trade secret, the party alleging the misappropriation shall identify the trade secret with reasonable particularity subject to any orders that may be appropriate under Section 3426.5 of the Civil Code."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 2019.210 (Leginfo official text), Cal. Civ. Proc. Code § 2019.210 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=2019.210.)
  Known gap: Reported California decisions may describe procedural consequences courts have imposed for noncompliance (such as staying or limiting discovery), but that question could not be verified in this session because the same CourtListener rate-limit error (125-request daily quota exhausted, HTTP 429) that blocked research for the "reasonable particularity" clause also blocked any search on this point. This clause is limited to what the statute's own text does and does not say.

PROTECTIVE MEASURES AVAILABLE UNDER THE COMPANION SECRECY-PRESERVATION STATUTE
Civil Code section 3426.5, the provision section 2019.210 cross-references, requires a court in an action under the Uniform Trade Secrets Act to preserve the secrecy of an alleged trade secret by reasonable means. The statute's text lists several examples of such means: granting protective orders in connection with discovery proceedings, holding in-camera hearings, sealing the records of the action, and ordering any person involved in the litigation not to disclose an alleged trade secret without prior court approval.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "a court shall preserve the secrecy of an alleged trade secret by reasonable means, which may include granting protective orders in connection with discovery proceedings, holding in-camera hearings, sealing the records of the action, and ordering any person involved in the litigation not to disclose an alleged trade secret without prior court approval."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 3426.5 (Leginfo official text), Cal. Civ. Code § 3426.5 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=3426.5.)
  Known gap: Section 3426.5's text states that a court "shall preserve the secrecy of an alleged trade secret by reasonable means" and lists examples using the word "may include," but it does not itself specify a procedure, motion, or timeline for a party to request one of these measures in connection with the section 2019.210 identification step specifically, and no case law on that interaction was verified in this session for the reasons stated in the companion clauses above.

RELATIONSHIP TO OTHER TRADE SECRET STATUTES IN THIS CORPUS
Section 2019.210 sits within the Civil Discovery Act's chapter on the methods and sequence of discovery, not within the Uniform Trade Secrets Act itself. Its text does not define "trade secret" or "misappropriation," does not state a limitations period, and does not create or limit any substantive claim or defense; it cross-references the Uniform Trade Secrets Act (Civil Code section 3426 et seq.) only to identify which actions it applies to, and cross-references Civil Code section 3426.5 only for the available secrecy-preservation orders.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "CHAPTER 5. Methods and Sequence of Discovery [2019.010 - 2019.210]"
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 2019.210, chapter heading (Leginfo official text), Cal. Civ. Proc. Code, Pt. 4, Tit. 4, Ch. 5 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=2019.210.)
  Known gap: This clause describes the statute's placement and cross-references as they appear on the two official Leginfo pages fetched for this document; it does not describe how this discovery-sequencing rule interacts procedurally with the substantive misappropriation definitions, the preemption doctrine, or the criminal trade secret statutes covered in this corpus's other documents, beyond noting that section 2019.210's own text does not address those subjects.

This Information Sheet was prepared by Jane Doe on January 1, 2026 in San Jose, California. It reflects a review of the official text of Code of Civil Procedure section 2019.210 and Civil Code section 3426.5 concerning a matter involving Acme Inc. and John Smith in Superior Court of California, County of Santa Clara, case number 24CV012345. Nothing in this Information Sheet is a trade secret identification statement, a discovery response, or a filing in that or any other action.
